passage: Throughout history, major scientific breakthroughs have often met fierce resistance not because the evidence was weak, but because the new findings threatened deeply entrenched worldviews. When Nicolaus Copernicus and later Galileo Galilei presented astronomical observations showing that Earth revolves around the Sun, their conclusions challenged centuries of philosophical authority and human self-importance. Similarly, nineteenth-century physicians initially ridiculed Ignaz Semmelweis when he demonstrated that simple handwashing dramatically reduced fatal infections in maternity wards, as accepting his data meant acknowledging that doctors themselves had been unintentionally harming patients. In both cases, objective facts collided with emotional attachment to established beliefs and professional pride. Progress in science therefore depends not only on gathering rigorous empirical evidence, but also on cultivating the intellectual humility required to revise cherished assumptions when reality demands it.
